knowledge_points.label: Pre-, mid-, post-training: from large low-quality to small high-quality data
knowledge_points.statement: Training proceeds through pre-training on raw text, mid-training on higher-quality data, and post-training on chat transcripts or RL, moving from large amounts of lower-quality data to small amounts of high-quality data; a base model is the result after pre- plus mid-training and an instruct/chat model the result after post-training.

anchors.quote: 1. Pre-training: train on raw text (e.g., documents from the web) ... 2. Mid-training: train more on high quality data to enhance capabilities ... 3. Post-training: train on chat transcripts or reinforcement learning ... large amounts of lower quality data to ... small amounts of high quality data.
Base model: after pre-training + mid-training ... Instruct/chat model: after post-training ... Increasingly, base models are not released
Example (OLMo from AI2) ... 1. **Pre-training** ... 2. **Mid-training** ... 3. **Post-training**
Data is fundamentally a long-tail problem, scales with human effort (unlike architectures, systems).
I want to argue that data is the most important thing to get right in language models. ... they don't say anything about their data.
One is that data is your competitive secret sauce. ... the second thing, which we'll talk a little bit more about, is copyright liability.

Data has always been a bottleneck, and always will be a bottleneck because it's in some sense a long-tail problem, and that scales with human effort. ... there's only so many people that can work on architectures and systems.
Then you move into mid-training where you train on more high quality data to enhance certain capabilities ... finally post training, where you're training on things like chat transcripts
The trend is that we go from training on large amounts of low quality data to smaller amounts of high quality data.
when we talk about the base model, This usually means after pre-training and mid training ... more recently, the largest models, there's no base model.

provenance.filtering_note: The motivation (L49-L63) argues data matters most because open-weight releases such as Llama 3 publish architecture and training procedure but 'basically no information on data' (L54), for two reasons: competitive dynamics and copyright liability (L58-L59). The OLMo 2 pre-training, Dolmino mid-training and Tulu 3 post-training mixtures (L81-L85) are images from the cited papers and are only shown; no mixture percentage is restated. The professor says the stage boundaries are blurry and there may be more stages (L69). Post-training data gets one image and one link (L84-L85) and is otherwise deferred to later lectures; the rest of this lecture is pre-training sources. Spoken evidence (1:55-2:18): why data scales with human effort and architectures and systems do not: 'there's only so many people that can work on architectures and systems', while data work for a broad model parallelizes ('[? paralyze ?]' in the captions), 'so that's why these data teams ... are actually quite big'. Spoken evidence (3:24-3:39): the base-model term is blurring, and for the largest models 'there's no base model', only the released instruct model (L77). Spoken evidence (2:23): the scope is set aloud, 'Today we're focusing mostly on pre-training'; post-training data is deferred to the next lecture (1:21:47).

misconceptions.belief: The data pipeline is one corpus: you collect the best text you can and train on it once.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The lecture names three stages with different data (raw web, high-quality, chat/RL) and a trend from large low-quality to small high-quality (L65-L72); the same tokens are not reused at every stage.

misconceptions.belief: A 'base model' is whatever comes out of pre-training alone.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor defines base model as after pre-training plus mid-training (L75); mid-training on high-quality data happens before the base checkpoint.

predict.q: A lab adds a stage between its raw-web pre-training and its chat fine-tuning. According to the lecture's trend, how should the data in this new stage compare with the pre-training data in volume and quality?
choices: smaller volume, higher quality
larger volume, higher quality
same volume, same quality but reshuffled
predict.why: Mid-training is 'train more on high quality data to enhance capabilities' and the trend across stages is from large amounts of lower-quality data to small amounts of high-quality data (L67, L70-L72).
predict.targets_misconception: The data pipeline is one corpus: you collect the best text you can and train on it once.

transfer.q: A model card lists 'checkpoint A: after web pre-training and a 50B-token textbook phase; checkpoint B: after SFT on conversations'. Using the lecture's terminology, name each checkpoint and say which one the professor notes is increasingly not released.
transfer.answer: A is the base model (pre-training + mid-training); B is the instruct/chat model (after post-training). Base models are increasingly not released.
transfer.why: L75-L77: base model is after pre-training plus mid-training, instruct/chat after post-training, and 'Increasingly, base models are not released'.
transfer.varies: a concrete model-card description replaces the abstract stage list (functional dimension)
transfer.invariant: the base/instruct boundary sits after mid-training, not after pre-training

check.q: A lab publishes a checkpoint taken right after its raw-web pre-training phase, before a planned phase of training on curated textbook and math data, and before any chat fine-tuning. In the lecture's terminology, what is this checkpoint?
choices: not yet the base model; that comes after mid-training
the base model; that comes right after pre-training
the instruct model; that comes before any fine-tuning
check.answer: not yet the base model; that comes after mid-training
check.why: L75: the base model is the result after pre-training plus mid-training; the curated textbook/math phase is mid-training (L67), so a checkpoint taken before it is not yet the base model. The instruct/chat model comes after post-training (L76).
check.varies: the checkpoint sits before mid-training rather than after it (inverse direction of the model-card item)
check.invariant: the base/instruct boundary: base = pre-training + mid-training, instruct = after post-training
check.targets_misconception: A 'base model' is whatever comes out of pre-training alone.
distractor_from: 'the base model; that comes right after pre-training' <- misconception: 'A 'base model' is whatever comes out of pre-training alone.'
'the instruct model; that comes before any fine-tuning' <- plausible: places the instruct label on the earliest usable checkpoint instead of after post-training

retrieval.q: Name the three training stages the lecture lists and the kind of data each uses.
retrieval.answer: Pre-training on raw text (web documents); mid-training on high-quality data; post-training on chat transcripts or reinforcement learning.

retrieval.q: What is the overall trend in data volume and quality across the stages of training?
retrieval.answer: From large amounts of lower-quality data to small amounts of high-quality data.

retrieval.q: Why, according to the professor, is data a 'long-tail problem' unlike architectures or systems?
retrieval.answer: Because it scales with human effort: curation and cleaning do not get solved once but keep demanding work.

knowledge_points.label: Live service → crawl → raw data: why 'the whole Internet' is not available
knowledge_points.statement: Models are not trained on 'the Internet' but on what a crawler could discover and download from live servers, which excludes dynamic app content, authenticated and paywalled content, and content blocked by robots.txt, bot detection, IP blocks and rate limits, and is further restricted legally by terms of service and copyright; the pipeline is live service → raw data → processed data.

anchors.quote: language models are trained on the entire Internet ... You can't train on live servers. ... A **crawler**: ... Discovers webpages (starting from a seed set) ... Downloads the discovered webpages

Dynamic content: ... Authentication: ... Technical restrictions: ... Not allowed to download some content based on `robots.txt` ... (voluntary) ... Legal restrictions: ... Terms of service (ToS) might prohibit downloading using bots
Decline of consent ... Examined restrictions (robots.txt, ToS) for URLs in common datasets (C4, RefinedWeb, Dolma) ... Restrictions have increased over time
Live service → raw data → processed data (transformation, filtering, deduplication)
language models are trained on the entire internet. ... So first of all, this doesn't really quite type-check.
So you can't actually train on these live servers unless you're training an RL agent.
One is that a lot of the web content is actually dynamic. ... it's not like you can just crawl Discord and get all the content on Discord.
There's actually huge amounts of content that are actually locked up behind these walled gardens. ... Or if you're X AI, you can train on X.
this is not a legal restriction, this is just like, you're supposed to be a good citizen and look at robots.txt.
websites have terms of service that say, if you go to a website, you have to obey this contract to use the website.
And the conclusion was that the restrictions have increased over time.
hitting their servers a million times in 24 hours ... this costs money for the person hosting it and also degrades service for everyone else trying to use it.
there's these things called shadow libraries, which are also part of the web. ... from a legal perspective, this is piracy and copyright infringement.
the internet is a huge and messy and scary place, and you can't actually get all of it.
at the top, the internet is a bunch of live services. ... Someone has to do the work of producing raw data

provenance.filtering_note: The professor refines 'Internet' to 'public (world wide) web' and then says even that is 'not quite right' (L92-L93). Examples given: Discord and wandb for dynamic apps; Facebook, X, LinkedIn, NYTimes for walled gardens (L109, L113). The Consent in Crisis trend figure (L128) and the Anthropic-crawling screenshot (L131) are shown, not restated; the professor's own gloss is that restrictions have increased over time and that crawlers that ignore ToS, robots.txt and server load impose costs on websites (L127, L132). Shadow libraries (L135-L143) are introduced here as 'technically part of the web' and are treated in books-provenance-spectrum and fair-use-training-vs-piracy. Spoken evidence (4:53-5:02): why 'trained on the entire internet' 'doesn't really quite type-check': the Internet is live services, and training on it would take 'an RL agent that goes on the internet and does stuff', which pre-training is not. Spoken evidence (7:21-7:26): walled gardens favour their owners: Facebook need not crawl Facebook, and 'if you're X AI, you can train on X'. Spoken evidence (10:39-11:12): his reading of the Consent in Crisis figure: robots.txt full restrictions roughly flat until 2023, then rising to 'almost 50%' in the plot, and most pages now carrying terms that forbid AI use; figure readings, not restated as facts. Spoken evidence (11:44-12:12): the crawling screenshot narrated: a site owner complaining of Anthropic's crawler 'hitting their servers a million times in 24 hours', Read the Docs also 'hammered'; he does not remember the site's name. Spoken evidence (1:19:49-1:20:11): the closing restates the pipeline: the Internet is live services, and someone (a site's dumps or a crawler) must produce the raw data before it is processed.

misconceptions.belief: A web crawl is a copy of the public web, so a Common Crawl-trained model has seen everything that is publicly reachable.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Pages behind JavaScript app state, logins, paywalls, robots.txt disallows, bot detection, IP blocks and rate limits are not downloaded (L105-L119); the crawl is what a polite crawler could fetch, not the web.

misconceptions.belief: robots.txt legally forbids crawling.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor marks robots.txt as 'voluntary' (L116); the legal restrictions are terms of service and copyright/licensing (L121-L123).

predict.q: A forum moves from server-rendered pages at distinct URLs to a single-page app where threads load after clicking, with the URL unchanged. Without any change to robots.txt or ToS, what happens to how much of its content a standard crawler captures?
choices: much less, because the content is now dynamic
the same, because the site is still public
more, because one URL now holds all threads
predict.answer: much less, because the content is now dynamic
predict.why: Dynamic content where 'URL doesn't change' and you 'need to click buttons and submit forms to access content' is the first category a crawler misses (L105-L109), independent of permissions.
predict.targets_misconception: A web crawl is a copy of the public web, so a Common Crawl-trained model has seen everything that is publicly reachable.

transfer.q: A research group argues it may freely train on a newspaper's articles because the newspaper's robots.txt does not list their crawler. Using the lecture's split between technical and legal restrictions, what is wrong with this argument?
transfer.answer: robots.txt is a voluntary technical signal, not a grant of rights; the legal questions are the site's terms of service and whether they hold a licence (or fair use) to copy the articles, which robots.txt does not answer.
transfer.why: L116 labels robots.txt '(voluntary)' under technical restrictions; L121-L123 put ToS and 'You might not have a license to copy the webpages (for training)' under legal restrictions.
transfer.varies: the restriction is absent rather than present (functional dimension: permission inferred from silence)
transfer.invariant: technical and legal restrictions are independent layers; passing one says nothing about the other

check.q: A news site's robots.txt disallows every crawler. A lab signs a licence with the publisher to train on its archive and receives the articles as a bulk export, never crawling the site. Using the lecture's split between technical and legal restrictions, which restriction still blocks training?
choices: none: robots.txt is a voluntary technical signal
robots.txt: it is a legal ban on using the pages
both robots.txt and copyright still forbid it
check.answer: none: robots.txt is a voluntary technical signal
check.why: robots.txt is listed under technical restrictions and is voluntary (L105-L123); it governs crawling, not rights. The legal layer (copyright, terms of service) is addressed by the licence, and no crawling happens.
check.varies: the lab holds a licence but robots.txt forbids crawling (inverse of 'robots.txt allows it, so it is legal')
check.invariant: robots.txt is a voluntary technical crawl signal; legal permission comes from licences, ToS and copyright
distractor_from: 'robots.txt: it is a legal ban on using the pages' <- misconception: 'robots.txt legally forbids crawling.'
'both robots.txt and copyright still forbid it' <- misconception: 'robots.txt legally forbids crawling.'

retrieval.q: What two things does a crawler do?
retrieval.answer: Discovers webpages starting from a seed set, and downloads the discovered webpages.

retrieval.q: Name two of the four categories of reasons the lecture gives for why one cannot simply download and train on all webpages.
retrieval.answer: Any two of: dynamic content; authentication (logins, paywalls); technical restrictions (robots.txt, bot detection, IP blocks, rate limits); legal restrictions (ToS, licences).

retrieval.q: What did the 'Consent in Crisis' study examine and what trend did it find?
retrieval.answer: robots.txt and ToS restrictions for the URLs in C4, RefinedWeb and Dolma; restrictions have increased over time.

knowledge_points.label: Copyright: automatic, low threshold, protects expression not ideas
knowledge_points.statement: Copyright attaches automatically to original works fixed in a tangible medium, with no registration needed and an extremely low threshold, so basically everything on the Internet is copyrighted; it protects expression rather than ideas and does not cover uncreative collections, and a copyrighted work may be used only with a licence or under fair use.

anchors.quote: Collections are not original works so hence not copyrightable (e.g., telephone directories) unless there is some creativity in the selection or arrangement ... Copyright applies to expression, not ideas (e.g., quicksort) ... Registration not required for copyright protection (in contrast with patents) ... Threshold for copyright is extremely low (e.g., your website is copyrighted)
Summary: *basically everything on the Internet are copyrighted.* ... How to use a copyrighted work: ... 1. Get a license for it. ... 2. Appeal to the fair use clause.
Goal: *incentivize* the creation of intellectual goods ... Goes back to 1709 in England (Statute of Anne) ... In United States, most recent: Copyright Act of 1976
Registration is required before creator can sue someone for copyright infringement ... Lasts for 75 years, and then the copyright expires and it becomes part of the public domain
the spirit of the law is to not just technically say no to everything, but to incentivize the creation of intellectual goods.
In particular, collections are not copyrightable. ... copyright applies to the expression, not the idea.
the barrier to getting a copyright was relaxed a lot. ... So it used to be that you had to publish something to have something copyright. ... Now things just have to be fixed.
But the threshold for copyright is very low. ... you put something on your website, it's copyrighted.
Now if you want to sue someone, you have to go get it registered, but it only costs $65. ... Which is much smaller than the lawyer fees that you'll probably pay
it lasts 75 years, and then the copyright expires. ... But after 75 years, presumably, it's not worth protecting, or they're passed away, or something.
So basically, everything on the internet is copyrighted. ... you either get a license for it, or B, you appeal to the fair use clause.

provenance.filtering_note: The professor gives a one-screen summary of US copyright: the 1976 Act's 'fixed in any tangible medium' language (L160), the 1909-to-1976 shift from 'published' to 'fixed' (L165), $65 registration (L170, cited to copyright.gov). The '75 years' duration at L171 is the professor's simplification; actual US terms depend on the work and date (inference, not in the lecture). Patents, trademarks and trade secrets are named as other IP types (L155) and dropped. Nothing here is specific to language models; the LM consequences come in fair-use-training-vs-piracy. Spoken evidence (17:42-17:59): registration before suing is no real barrier, '$65 ... much smaller than the lawyer fees', so the bar stays 'very low'. Spoken evidence (18:24-18:45): the rationale for a finite term: protection incentivizes creation, but 'after 75 years, presumably, it's not worth protecting, or they're passed away'; he repeats the 75-year simplification noted above. Spoken inconsistency (1:17:22): during Common Pile he says 'I think collections can be copyrighted', against his own 'collections are not copyrightable' (16:26) and L162; L162's exception (creativity in selection or arrangement) reconciles the two, and nothing is imported.

misconceptions.belief: Only works with a copyright notice or a registration are protected, so unlabelled web pages are free to copy.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Registration is not required for protection and the threshold is extremely low, so 'your website is copyrighted' (L166-L167); registration matters only before suing (L169).

misconceptions.belief: Reimplementing an algorithm from a paper infringes the paper's copyright.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Copyright applies to expression, not ideas; the lecture's example is quicksort (L163) and 'Reimplement an algorithm (the idea) rather than copying the code (the expression)' is listed as fair use (L201).

predict.q: A dataset builder scrapes a phone directory website (alphabetical listings) and a personal blog with no copyright notice. Under the lecture's rules, which one is copyrighted?
choices: the blog only
the phone directory only
both
neither
predict.why: Collections without creative selection or arrangement (telephone directories) are not copyrightable (L162), while the threshold for everything else is extremely low and needs no notice or registration (L166-L167).
predict.targets_misconception: Only works with a copyright notice or a registration are protected, so unlabelled web pages are free to copy.

transfer.q: A team wants to teach a model a sorting technique described in a 1995 textbook. Option A: paste the textbook's chapter into the training set. Option B: write their own explanation and examples of the technique. Which option sits on the 'idea' side of the lecture's idea/expression line, and why does the other one need a licence or fair use?
transfer.answer: Option B uses the idea (the technique), which copyright does not protect. Option A copies the author's expression (the chapter text), which is copyrighted and so needs a licence or a fair-use argument.
transfer.why: L163: copyright applies to expression, not ideas (quicksort example); L175-L177: a copyrighted work is usable only via a licence or fair use.
transfer.varies: from code (quicksort) to prose about an algorithm (modality dimension)
transfer.invariant: the protected object is the author's fixed expression, never the underlying method

check.q: A developer reads a paper that describes a new attention algorithm and writes an implementation from its equations, copying none of the paper's text or code. Under the lecture's copyright rules, what is the status of the implementation?
choices: infringing: the paper's algorithm is protected by its copyright
allowed: copyright covers the paper's expression, not its idea
allowed only because the paper has no copyright registration
check.answer: allowed: copyright covers the paper's expression, not its idea
check.why: L160-L167: copyright applies to expression, not ideas; the algorithm is the idea. Registration is irrelevant to whether copyright exists (it attaches automatically; L169 registration only matters before suing).
check.varies: the idea is an algorithm in a paper and the reuse is code, not a textbook chapter and training text
check.invariant: the idea/expression line: copyright protects the expression, not the underlying idea
check.targets_misconception: Reimplementing an algorithm from a paper infringes the paper's copyright.
distractor_from: 'infringing: the paper's algorithm is protected by its copyright' <- misconception: 'Reimplementing an algorithm from a paper infringes the paper's copyright.'
'allowed only because the paper has no copyright registration' <- misconception: 'Only works with a copyright notice or a registration are protected, so unlabelled web pages are free to copy.'

retrieval.q: What does copyright protect and what does it not protect, per the lecture's quicksort example?
retrieval.answer: It protects expression (the particular text or code), not ideas (the algorithm).

retrieval.q: What are the two ways the lecture gives for lawfully using a copyrighted work?
retrieval.answer: Get a licence for it, or appeal to the fair-use clause.

retrieval.q: Why is a telephone directory not copyrightable while a personal web page is?
retrieval.answer: A directory is a collection without creative selection or arrangement; the threshold for any original fixed work is extremely low, so an ordinary web page qualifies.

prompts.self_explain: Why does an extremely low copyright threshold make 'basically everything on the Internet' a problem specifically for pre-training, rather than for search engines that already index the same pages?

knowledge_points.label: Licences are promises not to sue; terms of service can still restrict use
knowledge_points.statement: A licence, from contract law, is a licensor's promise not to sue a licensee; Creative Commons licences enable free redistribution of copyrighted work and model developers also buy licences (Google–Reddit, OpenAI–Shutterstock, OpenAI–Stack Exchange), but terms of service can impose further restrictions, as when YouTube forbids downloading videos even if they are Creative Commons licensed.

anchors.quote: A license (from contract law) is granted by a licensor to a licensee. ... Effectively, 'a license is a promise not to sue'. ... The Creative Commons license enables free distribution of copyrighted work. ... Created by Lessig and Eldred in 2001 to bridge public domain and existing copyright
Many model developers license data for training foundation models ... Google and Reddit ... OpenAI and Shutterstock ... OpenAI and StackExchange

Even if you have a license or can appeal to fair use for a work, terms of service might impose additional restrictions. ... Example: YouTube's terms of service prohibits downloading videos, even if the videos are licensed under Creative Commons.
a license from contract law is something that a licensor grants to a licensee. ... It basically says, don't sue me.
there's a really nice license called Creative Commons, which allows something to act like it was in the public domain.
It was created in 2001 to essentially bridge public domain and existing copyright, because otherwise you have to wait 75 years.
So if you have money, you can pay someone to give you a license.

Remember that there's still terms of service that allow or prevent you from actually just getting a piece of work. ... YouTube has all these videos which are licensed, but the terms of service prohibits just downloading the videos using a bot
so the first license I believe you're still allowed to train on it. ... the license being changed means that you wouldn't be able to train on the later things.

provenance.filtering_note: The Creative Commons examples (Wikipedia, Open Courseware, Khan Academy, Free Music Archive, 307 million Flickr images, 39 million MusicBrainz images, 10 million YouTube videos, L184) are listed, not sourced; those counts are not used in prompts. The three licensing deals (L188-L190) are cited to press releases and news; the professor gives no deal terms. Later sections apply this KP: GitHub 'Allowed to train on any public repository with a permissive license (e.g., MIT, Apache)' (L305), arXiv authors choosing all-rights-reserved or CC with CC0 metadata (L325-L326), BooksCorpus taken down for violating Smashwords' ToS (L350). Spoken evidence (20:00-20:19): why Creative Commons exists: otherwise a creator who wants reuse leaves others waiting out the 75-year term; a CC licence makes the work 'act like it's in the public domain'. Spoken evidence (31:33-32:12, Q&A): if a licence is later made more restrictive, he believes ('I'm not a lawyer') content obtained under the old licence can still be trained on, but for a living source such as Reddit the change governs new content, so 'you wouldn't be able to train on the later things'.

prerequisites.note: A licence is the first of the two routes to using a copyrighted work (L176).

misconceptions.belief: If content is under a Creative Commons licence, any way of obtaining it for training is permitted.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Terms of service are a separate contract layer; YouTube forbids downloading videos even when they are CC licensed (L216-L217), and BooksCorpus was removed for violating Smashwords' ToS although the books were priced at $0 (L348-L350).

misconceptions.belief: A licence transfers ownership of the work.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The lecture defines a licence as a contract-law promise not to sue the licensee (L180-L181); the licensor keeps the copyright.

predict.q: A video platform's terms of service forbid downloading, but a creator uploads lectures under CC-BY. A lab bulk-downloads those lectures with a script. Which of the lecture's two legal layers has the lab violated?
choices: terms of service only
copyright only
both copyright and terms of service
neither, because CC-BY permits reuse
predict.why: The CC licence is a promise not to sue over copying (L181, L183), but 'terms of service might impose additional restrictions' and YouTube's ToS prohibits downloading even CC videos (L216-L217).
predict.targets_misconception: If content is under a Creative Commons licence, any way of obtaining it for training is permitted.

transfer.q: A company proposes to fetch every arXiv paper's title and abstract plus the full LaTeX source of papers marked 'all rights reserved' via the S3 bulk download. Using the lecture's licence framing, which part is clearly licensed for reuse and which part would need a licence or fair use?
transfer.answer: Titles and abstracts (metadata) are under a permissive CC0 licence and are usable; the LaTeX source of all-rights-reserved papers is copyrighted with no licence granted, so it needs a licence or a fair-use argument even though bulk download itself is offered.
transfer.why: L325-L326: authors choose all-rights-reserved or Creative Commons, and metadata is CC0; L175-L177: without a licence the remaining route is fair use. The availability of an S3 download (L327) is access, not permission.

knowledge_points.label: Fair use: four factors; courts so far say training is fair use, pirating copies is not
knowledge_points.statement: Fair use weighs purpose and character (transformative favoured), nature of the work, amount used, and market effect; for language models the professor notes that copying data is already the regulated act, that training should be transformative and about general ideas rather than concrete expression, and that in Bartz v. Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta training was held fair use while pirating books was not, so the area remains unsettled.

anchors.quote: Four factors to determine whether fair use applies: ... 1. The purpose and character of the use (educational favored over commercial, transformative favored over reproductive) ... 4. The effect of the use upon the market (or potential market) for the original work

Copying data (first step of training) is violation already even if you don't do anything with it. ... Training a model should be transformative (far from just copy/pasting). ... Model should be about the general idea (e.g., wizards), not in the concrete expression (e.g., Harry Potter).

Summary judgement (2025): training on plaintiff's works is fair use ... but pirating copies is not (even if don't train) ... Anthropic also bought and scanned the books; this is also fair use (but too late) ... Outcome: Anthropic paid $1.5B to authors to settle
So far training has been deemed fair use (for specific instances, but unclear in general) ... Pirating books is clearly illegal ... Still a very active, evolving area

Copyright is not about verbatim memorization: ... Plots and characters (e.g., Harry Potter) can be copyrightable ... Parody (imitating to make fun of something) is likely fair use ... Copyright is about semantics (and economics).
fair use says, I can use this anyway, even if I don't have a license, and these four factors determine whether fair use applies. ... They're just tendencies which have to be weighed in court

if you're trying to do something for education, it is more likely to be fair use than if you're trying to sell ... if you transform something, then that's going to be more favored than if you just literally host the identical copy.
if you take an author's work and you provide an alternative, and that decreases the amount that the original author could monetize their work
eventually meaning after 11 years-- this lawsuit was settled in favor of Google
One thing to note is that copyright is not about verbatim memorization. ... a lot of papers are focused on verbatim memorization.
It's definitely not about N-gram overlap, and also about the economics.
even the mere fact of copying-- which is in the word copyright-- is potentially a violation already ... This is not necessarily a fact, but intuitively has a transformative flavor.
regardless of copyright, language models can definitely affect the market. ... by negatively affecting the market, you are more likely to be ruled not fair use.
this was a landmark ruling that said, actually, this particular instance of training is fair use. ... However, Anthropic, you're still in trouble because you pirated all these books
you can't pirate and then buy it ... So the outcome is that Anthropic paid 1.5 billion to settle the authors. ... So this is about $3,000 a book.
training, so to speak, has been deemed of fair use, or at least has been not deemed not fair use. ... The rulings have so far been narrow.
most likely in Common Crawl, there are copyrighted books and content that you are not supposed to train on ... Books are not remarkably different from your website, for example. both are copyrighted.

Google, L199-L202) are illustrations. The NYT v. OpenAI allegation (L220-L221) is stated with no outcome. Kadrey v. Meta (L230-L233): training held fair use 'in this instance' (cited to TechCrunch), the torrenting allegation still pending. The professor's claim that 'Language models can definitely affect the market (writers, artists), regardless of copyright' (L213) is an opinion flagged as such. The shadow-library passage (L135-L143) supplies the piracy side: LibGen, Z-Library, Anna's Archive, Sci-Hub 'From a legal perspective, this is piracy and copyright infringement' (L142). Spoken evidence (21:42-21:51): the four factors are 'not hard rules ... just tendencies which have to be weighed in court'. Spoken evidence (24:39-24:47): copyright is not verbatim memorization, a point he flags as new 'for an ML audience' because 'a lot of papers are focused on verbatim memorization'. Spoken evidence (25:58-26:05): the transformative argument is hedged aloud: training 'is not necessarily a fact, but intuitively has a transformative flavor' (L211's 'should be transformative'). Spoken evidence (26:43-26:49): L213 is tied to factor 4: 'by negatively affecting the market, you are more likely to be ruled not fair use'. Spoken evidence (29:02-29:14): piracy is not cured by a later purchase ('you can't pirate and then buy it'), and the $1.5B settlement is 'about $3,000 a book' (consistent with the roughly 500,000 works covered by the Bartz settlement; author check). Spoken evidence (30:07): the rulings 'have so far been narrow'. Spoken evidence (44:08-44:58, Q&A): a crawl cannot be vetted for pirated books ('you can't'), so Common Crawl most likely contains copyrighted books, and a book differs from a website only in how easily its author can defend it in court; both are copyrighted. Unclear (27:55): on NYT v. OpenAI the captions read 'I don't think this is still pending'; L220-L221 give no outcome, and nothing is imported. On Meta's pending torrenting claim, 'if precedent holds, this is also not going to be good for Meta' (29:42) is his opinion.

prerequisites.note: Fair use is the second route (L177) and the idea/expression line (L163) is what 'wizards vs Harry Potter' (L212) applies.

knowledge_points.label: Common Crawl: monthly Nutch crawls from seed URLs under selection, politeness and re-visit policies
knowledge_points.statement: Common Crawl, a non-profit founded in 2007, runs a crawl roughly every month with Apache Nutch that adds 3-5 billion pages, starting from hundreds of millions of seed URLs and repeatedly popping a URL, downloading it and enqueuing its hyperlinks, governed by a selection policy (which pages), a politeness policy (robots.txt, server load) and a re-visit policy, with the challenge that many dynamic URLs lead to the same content.

anchors.quote: Common Crawl is a non-profit organization founded in 2007. ... Every ~month, run a web crawl (add 3-5 billion web pages) ... Crawls have some overlap but try to diversify ... 300 billion pages so far
Crawling uses Apache Nutch ... Starts with a set of seed URLs (at least hundreds of millions) ... Pop a URL from the queue, download URL, and add hyperlinks to queue

Selection policy: which pages to download? ... Politeness policy: respect robots.txt, don't overload server ... Re-visit policy: how often to check if pages change ... Challenge: URLs are dynamic, many URLs lead to basically same content
How many URLs are there? Hard to estimate, but O(billions) ... Google search index is at least 100 PB ... has 2.19 billion pages (372.2 TB)
So most model developers have their own crawler, because they want to have full control over what the data is.
And every month they run a web crawl, gets about three to five billion web pages. ... Each crawl has some overlap with the previous crawl, but they try to diversify and get new pages.
crawling is conceptually straightforward, but all the gory details are in the implementation. ... It's basically graph traversal.
you have to respect robots.txt, don't overload the server. ... you want a policy that will download frequently changed pages, but not spend time downloading pages that don't change.
many URLs might lead to the same content, so there's a lot of duplication that happens if you're not careful. ... In particular, mirror sites explicitly is about duplication.

provenance.filtering_note: The 2.19 billion pages / 372.2 TB figure for the April 2026 crawl (L251) and 'Google search index is at least 100 PB' (L250) are read off linked pages and are recorded as cited, not as facts to memorize. The crawler-architecture diagram (L254) is Wikimedia's generic figure. The professor does not describe how Common Crawl's selection policy chooses seeds or how overlap between monthly crawls is managed beyond 'try to diversify' (L246). Every later web dataset in the lecture (C4, Pile-CC, MassiveWeb, CCNet, RefinedWeb, FineWeb, Dolma, DCLM, Nemotron-CC) starts from these crawls. Spoken evidence (32:20): 'most model developers have their own crawler, because they want to have full control'; Common Crawl serves everyone else. Spoken evidence (34:55): mirror sites are a named source of URL-level duplication. Aside (33:01-33:08): he doubts the '300 billion pages' total against the monthly rate ('if you multiply this number by 20, you don't quite get 300 billion. But that's what they say'); the intended arithmetic is unclear, and L247's figure stays the source's.

prerequisites.note: The crawler definition (L99-L101) and the robots.txt/rate-limit restrictions (L116-L119) are what the politeness policy implements.

misconceptions.belief: Each monthly Common Crawl snapshot is a fresh copy of the whole web, so using more snapshots just means more passes over the same pages.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each crawl adds 3-5 billion pages, crawls 'have some overlap but try to diversify' (L245-L246), and the re-visit policy decides when to re-check pages (L261); later datasets use many dumps (FineWeb used 95, L515) precisely to get more distinct pages.

misconceptions.belief: A crawl queue is a list of pages; the number of URLs equals the number of distinct documents.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor flags that 'URLs are dynamic, many URLs lead to basically same content' (L262), which is why deduplication is a separate pipeline stage.

predict.why: Each crawl adds 3-5 billion pages and crawls 'have some overlap but try to diversify' (L245-L246).
predict.targets_misconception: Each monthly Common Crawl snapshot is a fresh copy of the whole web, so using more snapshots just means more passes over the same pages.

Name the crawler policy that handles each of these two issues and say what the professor calls the general challenge behind the first.

choices: selection policy
re-visit policy

knowledge_points.label: WARC vs WET: HTML-to-text extraction is lossy and changes downstream accuracy
knowledge_points.statement: Common Crawl ships WARC (raw HTTP responses, i.e. HTML) and WET (text already extracted by a lossy process); re-extracting text from WARC with a tool such as trafilatura, resiliparse or jusText changes the trained model's downstream accuracy, so The Pile, RefinedWeb and Nemotron-CC all start from WARC and choose their extractor deliberately.

anchors.quote: WARC: raw HTTP response (e.g., HTML) ... WET: converted to text (lossy process) ... Tools to convert HTML to text: trafilatura, resiliparse ... The conversion matters for the resulting LM's downstream task accuracy
Pile-CC: Common Crawl, use WARC, jusText to convert into text (better than WET)
trafilatura for HTML→text, extract content (WARC instead of WET files)
For HTML→text, used jusText (not trafilatura) because it returned more tokens
One is a WARC file. ... So this is the raw HTTP response.
They convert to a WET file, which is necessarily a loss-y process. ... the way you convert actually does matter.
you look at the web files that Common Crawl releases versus these other tools, and it seems like trafilatura and resiliparse are better.

provenance.filtering_note: The evidence that extraction matters is the DCLM figure images/dclm-wet.png (L271), which compares extractors by downstream accuracy; its numbers are the paper's and are not restated. The professor does not explain what WET's extractor drops (boilerplate handling, structure, math) or how trafilatura, resiliparse and jusText differ internally; the only stated difference is Nemotron-CC's reason for jusText, that it 'returned more tokens' (L563). Status is 'shown' because the central claim rests on the figure. Spoken evidence (35:32-36:08): WET 'is not necessarily the best way to use the web', and his qualitative reading of the DCLM ablation is that trafilatura and resiliparse beat the WET files; no number from the figure is restated. He still does not say what WET drops, and jusText is never mentioned aloud.

prerequisites.note: WARC and WET are the two formats the crawl is distributed in (L264).

misconceptions.belief: WET is just WARC with the HTML tags stripped, so the two carry the same text.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor calls WET a 'lossy process' (L266) and shows that the choice of extractor changes downstream accuracy (L270-L271); Pile-CC's re-extraction from WARC with jusText was 'better than WET' (L430).

misconceptions.belief: The best extractor is the one that produces the cleanest text.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Nemotron-CC picked jusText over trafilatura because it 'returned more tokens' (L563), trading cleanliness for volume; the lecture presents the extractor as a tunable choice judged by downstream accuracy and token yield, not by a single cleanliness criterion.

predict.q: Two teams build datasets from the same Common Crawl snapshot and apply identical filters and dedup. Team 1 uses the WET files; team 2 re-extracts text from WARC with trafilatura. According to the lecture, how will the downstream task accuracy of models trained on each compare?
choices: identical, because the underlying pages are the same
different, because HTML-to-text conversion is lossy and affects accuracy
team 1 higher, because WET is Common Crawl's official text
predict.answer: different, because HTML-to-text conversion is lossy and affects accuracy
predict.why: WET is 'converted to text (lossy process)' and 'The conversion matters for the resulting LM's downstream task accuracy' (L266, L270).
predict.targets_misconception: WET is just WARC with the HTML tags stripped, so the two carry the same text.

transfer.q: A team is short on tokens and must pick between an extractor that yields cleaner main-body text and one that yields 20% more text per page. Which dataset in the lecture faced this choice, what did it pick and why, and what would you measure before trusting that choice for your own model?
transfer.answer: Nemotron-CC chose jusText over trafilatura because it returned more tokens, while explicitly trying to preserve quality; before copying that choice you would compare downstream task accuracy of models trained on each extraction, which is the criterion the DCLM comparison used.
transfer.why: L561-L563: Nemotron-CC wanted more tokens and chose jusText for yield; L270-L271: the extractor comparison is judged by downstream accuracy.
transfer.varies: the objective shifts from accuracy alone to accuracy under a token budget (functional dimension)
transfer.invariant: extraction is a pipeline choice evaluated by its effect on the trained model, not by text appearance

check.q: A team compares two HTML-to-text extractors on the same WARC files. Extractor X gives text that looks cleaner to human readers; extractor Y keeps more text per page. By the criterion the lecture's DCLM comparison uses, how should they choose?
choices: pick X, since the cleanest text makes the best training data
train a model on each output and compare downstream accuracy
pick Y, since more tokens always make the better training data
check.answer: train a model on each output and compare downstream accuracy
check.why: L264-L271: the HTML-to-text conversion matters for the resulting LM's downstream accuracy, which is what the DCLM figure compares. Neither cleanliness nor token yield alone is the criterion; Nemotron-CC chose jusText for yield while trying to preserve quality (L563).
check.varies: the team chooses between extractors before training rather than explaining a past choice
check.invariant: extraction is lossy and its effect is measured by downstream accuracy of the trained model
check.targets_misconception: The best extractor is the one that produces the cleanest text.
distractor_from: 'pick X, since the cleanest text makes the best training data' <- misconception: 'The best extractor is the one that produces the cleanest text.'
'pick Y, since more tokens always make the better training data' <- plausible: over-generalises Nemotron-CC's token-yield choice into a rule

retrieval.q: What do WARC and WET files each contain?
retrieval.answer: WARC: the raw HTTP response (HTML). WET: text converted from it by a lossy process.

retrieval.q: Name two HTML-to-text tools the lecture links and one dataset that used each.
retrieval.answer: trafilatura (RefinedWeb), resiliparse (linked as a tool); jusText (Pile-CC, Nemotron-CC).

retrieval.q: Why did Nemotron-CC use jusText rather than trafilatura?
retrieval.answer: It returned more tokens.

knowledge_points.label: Wikipedia, GitHub, arXiv, Stack Exchange: bulk dumps with metadata, no crawling needed
knowledge_points.statement: Specialised sources are obtained differently from the web: Wikipedia publishes periodic dumps, GitHub repositories are cloned via the git protocol with issues and PRs from the GitHub Archive event stream (or repositories from Software Heritage), arXiv offers S3 bulk download of PDF and LaTeX, and Stack Exchange publishes anonymised XML dumps with metadata, so none needs a crawler and each carries metadata and a licence status usable for filtering.

anchors.quote: Does not contain original thought (no opinions, promotions, personal web pages, etc.) ... Includes articles based on notability ... Produce periodic dumps every few weeks (no need to crawl)

Lots of duplicates (e.g., copied code, forks, etc.) ... Allowed to train on any public repository with a permissive license (e.g., MIT, Apache) ... Repository: download through git protocol (rather than scraping the GitHub website) ... Metadata: GitHub API provides issues, pull requests, comments, etc.

Submission: metadata, PDF, LaTeX source (optional) ... Authors choose (i) all rights reserved or (ii) Creative Commons (e.g., CC-BY) ... Metadata (title, abstract) is under a permissive license (CC0) ... Bulk download from Amazon S3, no need to crawl
Q&A format is close to instruction tuning / real application ... Note: there is metadata (users, votes, comments, badges, tags) for filtering ... Data dumps in XML (anonymized, include metadata)
Aside: data poisoning attacks ... can inject malicious edits right before periodic dumps happen before edits are rolled back ... Takeaway: even high quality sources might contain bad content
the web is not a uniform place. ... There are specific pockets of really interesting, high quality content
You can't have original thought in it, because everything has to be referenced and cited. ... they can also cite books
every few weeks, they do a periodic dump. ... So this is important because you don't need to crawl Wikipedia. ... In fact, they don't want you to crawl Wikipedia.
these periodic dumps happen at a regular cadence. ... the dump still has the malicious content.
if you consider adversaries, even so-called high quality contents might contain bad things in them. ... I think this has been fixed since then.
code is important not just for if you want coding capabilities for your language model, but if you want general reasoning.
There's the repository data, which you can just go and download through the GitHub Git protocol. ... you shouldn't scrape GitHub, you should just download the repository.
what does it mean to train on arXiv? ... you have to convert the PDF into text, or you can use the LaTeX source
And I think most arXiv papers are Creative Commons.
this is quite close to a real application. ... So not everything is super magically emergent. ... this data has metadata, which is like the number of votes which are useful for filtering.

provenance.filtering_note: Size statistics (Wikipedia 67 million articles in 361 editions, GitHub 420M+ repositories with 28M public, arXiv ~3M submissions, Software Heritage 28.8M source files, L280, L302, L315, L322) are read from linked pages as of May 2026 and are cited only. Software Heritage (L311-L315) is noted as a non-profit aggregating GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and PyPI that keeps repositories but not issues/comments. The poisoning aside (L291-L294) cites two papers; the mechanism is an edit timed before a dump. The link labelled 'GitHub Archive' at L309 points at the arXiv S3 page (source typo). The professor's claim that code helps reasoning is marked '(folklore)' (L298). Spoken evidence (37:03-37:21): Wikipedia is not just a rewrite of the web, since its citations include books. Spoken evidence (38:24): Wikipedia does not want to be crawled; the dump is the intended route. Spoken evidence (39:44): the dump-timing poisoning 'has been fixed since then', he thinks. Spoken evidence (42:21-42:36): 'what does it mean to train on arXiv?': PDF-to-text or the LaTeX source, a design choice (LLaMA used LaTeX, L496). Spoken evidence (57:23-57:48): Stack Exchange shows that parts of the web already look supervised, so 'not everything is super magically emergent': question-answer behaviour has direct examples in pre-training data. Spoken note (39:50): code's benefit for 'general reasoning' is stated without L298's '(folklore)' hedge; the hedge is kept. Spoken slip (43:01): 'I think most arXiv papers are Creative Commons'. L325 gives authors the choice without proportions; arXiv's default, and by public tallies the large majority, is arXiv's own non-exclusive distribution licence, not CC (one Open Knowledge Foundation tally: about 3.4% of uploads since 2015 chose a non-default licence; author check, not imported).

prerequisites.note: 'No need to crawl' (L289, L327) is the contrast with the crawler route of L99-L101.

misconceptions.belief: High-quality curated sources such as Wikipedia can be trusted as-is and need no filtering.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor's aside shows that malicious edits injected right before a periodic dump end up in the dump before they are reverted; 'even high quality sources might contain bad content' (L292-L294).

knowledge_points.label: Quality by resemblance: Reddit karma, Wikipedia-likeness and classifier reference sets
knowledge_points.statement: Web datasets define 'quality' by resemblance to a trusted reference: WebText kept pages linked from Reddit posts with at least 3 karma, CCNet kept documents that look like Wikipedia under a KenLM 5-gram model, GPT-3 trained a classifier to separate WebText/Wikipedia/Books from the rest, LLaMA classified pages by whether Wikipedia references them, and DCLM trained a fastText classifier on OpenHermes-2.5 and ELI5 positives against RefinedWeb negatives, which outperformed other filters.

anchors.quote: Contains pages that are outgoing links from Reddit posts with ≥ 3 karma (surrogate for quality) ... 8 million pages, 40GB text
Quality filtering: keep documents that look like Wikipedia under a KenLM 5-gram model ... Trained BERT models, CCNet(CommonCrawl) outperforms Wikipedia
Trained quality classifier to distinguish {WebText, Wikipedia, Books1, Books2} from rest
CommonCrawl processed with CCNet, classify *references* of Wikipedia or not

Positive examples (200K): ... OpenHermes-2.5: mostly GPT-4 generated instruction data ... ELI5: subreddit with curiosity questions and answers ... Negative examples (200K): ... RefinedWeb ... Trained a fastText classifier, run it on all of DCLM-pool ... This quality classifier outperforms other filtering methods
you look at pages that are outgoing links from Reddit posts with greater than three karma. ... So a good post must link to good websites.
they wanted to keep documents that look like Wikipedia. ... you score a probability of a new document under that language model to gauge how Wikipedia-like it was.
because you can get much more data, you can actually outperform just training on Wikipedia.
So they were able to get, using this method, 17gb of text using 12 Common Crawl dumps. ... which means that Common Crawl is maybe incomplete
they trained a quality classifier to distinguish things they deemed to be high quality from the rest
whether the page was a reference of Wikipedia, not whether it is actually a Wikipedia article. ... maybe Wikipedia articles are too stylized.
they took OpenHermes, which is essentially instruction data that was generated by GPT-4, and ELI5 ... So it's kind of weird, but somehow this works.
So the negative examples are anything from RefinedWeb ... They train a fastText classifier-- think about it just as a linear classifier.

provenance.filtering_note: OpenWebText replicated WebText by extracting URLs from the Reddit submissions dataset, filtering non-English with fastText and removing near duplicates (L358-L361). C4's 'WebText-like' experiment filtered 12 dumps to OpenWebText links and got 17 GB versus WebText's 40 GB, which the professor reads as 'suggesting CommonCrawl is incomplete' (L402-L403); that improved GLUE/SQuAD (L404). The DCLM quality figure images/dclm-quality.png (L556) carries the comparison numbers and is only shown; 'outperforms other filtering methods' is the professor's gloss. CCNet's motive was more data for low-resource languages such as Urdu (L367). The professor does not discuss the circularity of defining quality as 'looks like what we already trust'; that is left to the learner's self-explain prompt. Spoken evidence (47:20): the WebText rationale, 'a good post must link to good websites'. Spoken evidence (1:00:19-1:00:32): why LLaMA scored references of Wikipedia rather than Wikipedia-likeness: 'maybe Wikipedia articles are too stylized', while the pages they cite are 'presumably good'. Spoken evidence (1:06:39-1:06:56): of DCLM's instruction-data positives, 'it's kind of weird, but somehow this works', and the fastText model is 'just ... a linear classifier'. Spoken evidence (50:08-50:26): the motive for all these proxies: small datasets were clean, Common Crawl was 'a mess', and training on it 'led to junk results'. Spoken slip (47:20, 51:49): 'greater than three karma'; L355 and Radford et al. say at least 3; not imported.

prerequisites.note: Each of these filters selects from Common Crawl pages.
Wikipedia and Reddit, the reference sets, were introduced as curated sources before being used as positives.

external_prerequisites.note: A filter that changes which pages are kept changes the data distribution; lecture 9 argues such changes shift a scaling law's offset, so a small-scale ranking of filters (the DCLM comparison) is expected to persist at scale.

misconceptions.why_wrong: Every filter in the lecture operationalises quality as similarity to a chosen reference: Reddit-linked pages (L355), Wikipedia under KenLM (L372), a classifier trained on WebText/Wikipedia/Books (L417), or OpenHermes/ELI5 (L547-L549); change the reference and 'quality' changes.

knowledge_points.label: Rule-based filtering: C4 and Gopher/MassiveWeb heuristics and what they discard
knowledge_points.statement: Because 'Common Crawl is mostly not useful natural language', C4 applied manual heuristics (keep lines ending in punctuation with at least 5 words, drop pages with fewer than 3 sentences, any bad word, a '{', 'lorem ipsum' or 'terms of use', and non-English by langdetect at 0.99) to go from 1.4 trillion tokens of one snapshot to 156 billion tokens, and Gopher's MassiveWeb used rules such as 80% of words containing an alphabetic character plus Google SafeSearch for toxicity instead of word lists.

anchors.quote: Observation: Common Crawl is mostly not useful natural language ... Started with one snapshot (April 2019) of Common Crawl (1.4 trillion tokens) ... Keep lines that end in punctuation and have >= 5 words ... Remove page with fewer than 3 sentences ... End result: 806 GB of text (156 billion tokens)

Removed page that contains any 'bad words' ... Removed page containing '{' (no code), 'lorem ipsum', 'terms of use', etc. ... Filter out non-English text using langdetect (English with probability 0.99)

Quality filtering using manual rules (not classifier) - e.g., 80% words contain at least one alphabetic character ... Use Google SafeSearch for toxicity (not word lists) ... Result: 10.5 TB of text (though Gopher only trained on 300B tokens - 12%)
URL filtering, language ID (keep if p(en) > 0.65) ... Filtering: Gopher, C4, more manual rules
Common Crawl is mostly not useful for natural language. ... any attempt to train on Common Crawl just led to junk results.
let's just define a bunch of rules, which turned out to be fairly effective. ... they keep lines that end in punctuation, that have more than five words, remove pages with fewer than three sentences
Interestingly, remove the curly brace, which filters out a lot of code-- so clearly at that time, they weren't thinking about code models
The end result is that you have 156 billion tokens, so 800 gigabytes of text.
their quality filtering was also based on manual rules. ... And part of the reason for this is that they had more control over that.
there is this division between people who wanted to use rules, and people who wanted to use classifiers. ... their model was only trained on a very small fraction of this dataset.

provenance.filtering_note: The 1.4T-in / 156B-out figures (L387, L396) and Gopher's 10.5 TB vs 300B tokens '12%' (L486) are the professor's text() readings of the T5 and Gopher papers; the retention ratio 156/1400 ≈ 11% follows by one division and is used in a prompt. The C4 domain analysis (Dodge et al.) is an image (L399) whose top-domain list is not restated. Gopher's other components (books, news, GitHub, Wikipedia) get 'no details' (L476-L479). FineWeb's language threshold p(en) > 0.65 (L516) is a looser rule than C4's 0.99 (L394) and is used as a contrast. The bad-words list is cited to the LDNOOBW GitHub repo (L392). RefinedWeb and Dolma reuse 'Gopher rules' (L509, L533). Spoken evidence (51:02-51:17): the '{' rule 'filters out a lot of code', showing 'at that time, they weren't thinking about code models'; this supports the why_wrong of the second misconception. Spoken evidence (59:03-59:25): why Gopher used rules: 'they had more control over that'; he frames a 'division between people who wanted to use rules, and people who wanted to use classifiers'. Aloud C4 is 156B tokens, 'so 800 gigabytes' (L396: 806 GB), and the line rule is 'more than five words' (50:42) where L390 says '>= 5 words'; an off-by-one in speech, not imported.

prerequisites.note: The rules are applied to one Common Crawl snapshot (L387).
Line- and sentence-level rules operate on extracted text, so what the extractor dropped is already gone.

external_prerequisites.note: C4 is reported both as 806 GB and as 156 billion tokens (L396); relating the two is the bytes-per-token compression ratio from lecture 1.

misconceptions.why_wrong: C4 went from 1.4 trillion to 156 billion tokens, keeping roughly a ninth (L387, L396), and the professor's framing is that Common Crawl 'is mostly not useful natural language' (L385).

misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor annotates it '(no code)' (L393): the rule encodes a content decision that excludes code, which later datasets (The Pile, LLaMA, The Stack) deliberately add back.

knowledge_points.statement: A training-token count reported for a model (Llama 3's 15T, Qwen3's 36T) counts every pass over the data, so with repetition it overstates the unique tokens: e epochs over U unique tokens are reported as e·U, and comparing a dataset's size (unique tokens, such as Nemotron-CC's 6.3T) with a model's training tokens therefore needs the number of epochs.

Like if you do two epochs, that's twice the number of tokens, so you have to be careful when you look at those numbers.' knowledge_points.label: Code data: The Stack and Stack v2 filter by licence, dedup, and linearise PRs
knowledge_points.statement: The Stack took repository names from the GitHub Archive (2015-2022), cloned 137M repositories (51B files, 5B unique), kept only permissively licensed ones (MIT, Apache) using go-license-detector and removed near-duplicates with minhash and Jaccard similarity to get 3.1 TB of code; Stack v2 drew repositories from Software Heritage and issues/PRs from the GitHub Archive, removed binaries, malware, bot activity and PII, paired low-resource languages with LLVM IR, added existing datasets such as GSM8K and OpenWebMath, and linearised pull requests into token sequences with inline file context.

anchors.quote: Took repository names from GitHub Archive (2015-2022) ... git clone'd 137M repositories, 51B files (5B unique!) ... Kept only permissively licensed (MIT, Apache) using go-license-detector ... Result: 3.1 TB of code

Repositories from the Software Heritage ... Processing: remove binary files, malware, bot activity, deduplication, PII redaction, subsample PRs ... Pair source code (especially low-resource languages like Nim) with shared low-level intermediate language (LLVM) ... Include existing datasets (GSM8K, code contests, StackOverflow, arXiv, Wikipedia, OpenWebMath)
Pull requests: ... Linearize structured object to token sequence ... Add some inline context (e.g., file surrounding diff), subsample
Code is helpful for programming tasks, but also for reasoning (folklore).
since it was clear by 2022 that coding was going to be really important.
So what they did in the initial version is that they clone 137 repos. ... They kept the ones that were permissively licensed, remove near-duplicates
So in GitHub repos, you have binary files which you probably don't want to train on. ... A lot of GitHub, especially these PRs, are bots, so you have to filter that.

they compile this code into a low-level intermediate language, LLVM ... the language model can actually learn the mapping between the shared low level representation, which has a lot of data on, and the thing that it does has less data on.
pull requests and all the metadata is not, by its nature, a linearized sequence. ... So one important thing you have to decide is how much context to provide.
So it's not just learning how to generate code, but also the software development process around code.

knowledge_points.label: Common Pile: training on permissively licensed data only, and why licences are subtle
knowledge_points.statement: Common Pile asks whether a good model can be trained only on permissively licensed data, collecting 8TB of it; the professor's reading is that the result 'can do decently, but tough to compete without more tokens', and that licence status is subtle because of licence laundering (copyrighted work redistributed under a permissive licence), collection licences such as Dolma's ODC-By that do not extend to individual documents, and the unclear status of synthetic data from models trained on unlicensed data.

anchors.quote: Almost all data on the Internet is copyrighted. ... Some of it is permissively licensed. ... Fair use of copyrighted content is not settled. ... Key question: can you train a good model using only permissively-licensed data?
CommonPile ... Collected 8TB dataset of permissively licensed data

License laundering: redistribute copyrighted work under permissive license (hard to detect) ... Collection licenses (Dolma is ODC-By) doesn't extend to individual ... Synthetic data from LMs trained on unlicensed data is unclear
Can do decently, but tough to compete without more tokens
So the question is, what about model-generated, like synthetic data? ... The short answer is probably yes.
if you're very, very risk-averse, then you say, well, if I don't know whether it is OK, that's a no. ... So can you train a good model with only permissively licensed data?
It turns out that a lot of government proceedings are actually permissively licensed
So in the end, there were 8 terabytes of data, which is actually pretty good for permissively licensed data.
So people are sloppy with licenses. ... So people might take some copyright work and just slap a CC BY on it.
But collection licenses don't extend to the individual works. ... But if you dig deeper, it's actually not permissively licensed at the individual level.

they also made a decision to forego training on any synthetic data ... So probably it's fine because technically, these are open weight models with MIT license. ... So it's a little bit of data laundering if you are really honest here.
I would say it's not as good as the Qwen models for sure ... it's still pretty tough to compete without doing more tokens.

provenance.filtering_note: The Common Pile source breakdown (images/commonpile.png, L609) and the Comma model results (images/comma-results.png, L617) are figures; which baselines Comma matched or trailed is not restated, only the professor's one-line gloss (L618). Status is 'shown' because the empirical conclusion rests on that figure. The professor does not define 'permissively licensed' here beyond the earlier MIT/Apache and CC examples. The lecture's closing summary (L41-L45) adds 'Data does not fall from the sky', the pipeline line, and 'Much of this pipeline is heuristic, many opportunities to improve!'. Spoken evidence (1:15:08-1:15:19): the Common Pile stance is risk aversion: 'if I don't know whether it is OK, that's a no.' Spoken evidence (1:15:54): government proceedings are a large permissive source (his reading of the source figure). Spoken evidence (1:17:52-1:18:27): the synthetic-data argument both ways: Common Pile skipped synthetic data; using it is 'probably ... fine' because open-weight models carry MIT licences, but those models 'were presumably also trained on unlicensed data', so 'it's a little bit of data laundering'; in Q&A (43:39-43:45) his short answer on synthetic data was 'probably yes'. Spoken evidence (1:18:36-1:19:21): reading the Comma results, it is 'not as good as the Qwen models for sure' but beats old 2023 baselines (the first Llama, MPT), and 'I think you can probably eke more out' of permissive data; no number is restated. Spoken note (1:17:22): 'I think collections can be copyrighted' (see copyright-low-threshold-expression's note).

prerequisites.note: 'Permissively licensed' and collection licences depend on the licence definition (L180-L185).
'Fair use of copyrighted content is not settled' (L604) is why a permissive-only dataset is interesting.
'Tough to compete without more tokens' (L618) is the token-count side of the same trade-off.

misconceptions.belief: If a dataset is released under an open licence (e.g. ODC-By), every document in it is licensed for training.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor notes that collection licences such as Dolma's ODC-By do not extend to the individual documents (L614); the collection's licence covers the compilation, not the copyright in each page.

misconceptions.belief: Text found on a site that labels it permissively licensed can be trusted as permissively licensed.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Licence laundering, redistributing copyrighted work under a permissive licence, is 'hard to detect' (L613), so the label on the redistributor's page is not proof.

transfer.q: To grow a permissive-only corpus, a team generates synthetic textbooks with a strong model trained on ordinary web data, and also scrapes a mirror site that relabels novels as CC-BY. Name the lecture's subtlety that applies to each addition.
transfer.answer: The synthetic textbooks fall under 'synthetic data from LMs trained on unlicensed data is unclear'; the relabelled novels are licence laundering, redistribution of copyrighted work under a permissive licence, which is hard to detect.
transfer.why: L613 and L615 state the two subtleties; Nemotron-CC's rephrasing (L569-L571) is the lecture's example of synthetic pretraining data whose provenance traces back to unlicensed training.
transfer.varies: two concrete growth strategies replace the abstract list of subtleties (functional dimension)
transfer.invariant: the licence status of training data is inherited from the provenance of the underlying work, not from the label at the point of collection

check.why: L612-L615: licence laundering is redistributing copyrighted work under a permissive licence, which is hard to detect. The MIT label does not license text the repository owner had no rights to.
check.varies: the laundered text sits inside a code repository rather than on a novel-mirror site
check.invariant: a permissive label is only as good as the labeller's rights; licence status is subtle

'none: the repository's MIT licence covers it' <- misconception: 'Text found on a site that labels it permissively licensed can be trusted as permissively licensed.'
